aliases: The Fourth Crusade's capture of Constantinople

location: Constantinople (Byzantine capital), with the earlier diversion to Zara (Zadar) on the Dalmatian coast

date.note: The Fourth Crusade was proclaimed by Pope Innocent III in 1198. Its leaders contracted with Venice in 1201 for transport; unable to pay in full, the army attacked the Christian city of Zara in November 1202, sailed to Constantinople in 1203 on behalf of the Byzantine claimant Alexios Angelos, and took the city a first time in July 1203. After relations broke down, the crusaders and Venetians stormed Constantinople on 12-13 April 1204 and sacked it over the following days. Baldwin of Flanders was crowned Latin emperor in May 1204; the Latin Empire lasted until the Byzantine recovery of the city in 1261.

summary: The Sack of Constantinople was the capture and plunder of the Byzantine capital in April 1204 by the army of the Fourth Crusade and its Venetian allies, after an expedition proclaimed for the East had been diverted first to Zara and then to Constantinople. It led to the creation of a Latin Empire and a Latin patriarchate in the city, and historians such as Steven Runciman, as well as Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew, have described it as deepening the estrangement between the Latin and Greek churches, while Henry Chadwick treats it as one stage in a longer estrangement extending to the Council of Florence; whether the diversion resulted from accident or design is debated.
description:
Pope Innocent III proclaimed a new crusade in 1198, aimed at the recovery of Jerusalem, which Saladin had taken in 1187. Its leaders agreed with Venice in 1201 for ships and supplies; Villehardouin, one of the leaders, records that 'the sum of these payments indicated above amounts to 85,000 marks'. Far fewer crusaders reached Venice than had been planned, and Robert of Clari, a knight of the rank and file, reports that after the army's payment '36,000 marks still remained due'. To defer the debt the army helped Venice take Zara, a Christian city under the king of Hungary, in November 1202, despite a prohibition delivered in the pope's name ('I forbid you, in the name of the Pope at Rome, to attack this city', as Villehardouin reports a Cistercian abbot saying); Innocent III excommunicated those who took part; he later absolved the crusaders, while the Venetians remained under excommunication. At Zara envoys of Alexios Angelos, son of the deposed emperor Isaac II and brother-in-law of Philip of Swabia, offered money, supplies, and troops if the army restored his father, and, in Villehardouin's words, promised that 'he will put all the empire of Romania under the obedience of Rome'.

The fleet reached Constantinople in June 1203 and took the city in July; the emperor Alexios III fled, and Isaac II was restored with his son as co-emperor Alexios IV. Alexios IV could not pay what had been promised, hostility grew between the Latins and the city's population, and in early 1204 he was overthrown and killed by Alexios V Doukas (Mourtzouphlos). The crusaders and Venetians then agreed in March 1204 how to divide the empire and its booty among themselves. Before the final assault, according to Robert of Clari, the bishops preached that 'the Greeks were traitors and murderers', that they 'were worse than Jews', and that they had withdrawn from obedience to Rome, and promised that 'by the authority of God and in the name of the pope, they would absolve all who attacked the Greeks'. The city fell on 12-13 April 1204 and was sacked over the following days. The Byzantine historian and official Niketas Choniates, an eyewitness, describes the desecration of Hagia Sophia: the altar 'was broken into bits and distributed among the soldiers', and a woman 'sat in the patriarch's seat, singing an obscene song and dancing'; he describes 'the groaning of men, the shrieks of women, wounds, rape, captivity, the separation of those most closely united', and he calls the attackers 'precursors of Anti-Christ', and he contrasts their conduct with the restraint he attributes to the Muslim conquerors of Jerusalem in 1187. Large numbers of relics and works of art were carried to the West; the Cistercian Gunther of Pairis narrates how his abbot Martin took relics from a Constantinopolitan church.

In May 1204 Baldwin of Flanders was crowned emperor in Hagia Sophia, and a Venetian, Thomas Morosini, became the Latin patriarch of Constantinople. Byzantine successor states formed at Nicaea, in Epirus, and at Trebizond, and in 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos recovered Constantinople from Nicaea, though the restored empire never regained its former extent. Innocent III, who had forbidden attacks on Christians, at first welcomed the prospect of the Greek church's union with Rome and then sharply reproached the crusaders when he learned of the sack.

Two scholarly debates frame the event. The first concerns the diversion. Donald Queller and Thomas Madden argue that it resulted from a chain of contingent decisions, driven above all by the shortfall in the Venetian contract and the offer of Alexios Angelos, against older theories of design that attributed the diversion to a plan by Venice (including a once-proposed compact between Venice and Egypt, drawn from the Old French Estoire d'Eracles), by Philip of Swabia, or by the papacy; Michael Angold and Jonathan Harris set the event within a longer history of hostility and mutual suspicion between Byzantium and the crusading West. The second concerns its effects on the churches. Steven Runciman traced the breach to long divergences of tradition brought to a head by the Normans, the reform papacy, and the crusades, and he gives the Fourth Crusade a decisive place in turning the division into popular enmity in the East; Henry Chadwick follows the making of the rift over a longer span down to the Council of Florence (1438-1445), in which 1204 is one stage of an estrangement already advanced before it and the failed unions of Lyons (1274) and Florence are later ones. In a greeting of 12 May 2004, marking the eight-hundredth anniversary, Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew wrote that 'some historians have expressed the opinion that the Fourth Crusade and the temporary establishment of a Western hierarchy by Rome in the East may truly mark the beginning of the schism', and that 'there is no doubt that the tragedy of the Fourth Crusade deepened the animosity between the Christian West and the Christian East especially among the laity'. Eight centuries later, in an address to Archbishop Christodoulos of Athens on 4 May 2001, Pope John Paul II spoke of 'the disastrous sack of the imperial city of Constantinople, which was for so long the bastion of Christianity in the East', said that 'the fact that they were Latin Christians fills Catholics with deep regret', and, referring to sins of Catholics 'by action or omission' against 'their Orthodox brothers and sisters', prayed 'may the Lord grant us the forgiveness we beg of him'. In his greeting of May 2004 Bartholomew answered that 'we recognize the Pope's sincerity and we honor his request for forgiveness'.
editorial_notes: This entry is filed under christianity because both parties, the Latin crusaders and Venetians and the Greek Byzantines, were Christian; the filing is a storage convention per ADR-0010, not a claim that the event belongs to either church, and both the Latin and the Greek perspectives are presented in their own voices (neutrality #11). NEUTRALITY: the Latin side is represented by Villehardouin (a leader, whose account is favorable to the leadership), Robert of Clari (a knight of the rank and file), and Gunther of Pairis, and the Greek side by Niketas Choniates, an eyewitness and Byzantine official. The polemical language on each side, the bishops' sermons calling the Greeks 'traitors and murderers' and 'worse than Jews' (as reported by Robert of Clari) and Choniates' description of the Latins as 'precursors of Anti-Christ', is quoted strictly as attributed language, never adopted in editorial voice. No figure for the dead is given because none of the sources read for this entry supplies one. The 'accident versus design' debate over the diversion and the question of the sack's role in the schism are presented as competing scholarly framings without adjudication (neutrality #2). John Paul II's 2001 statement and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew's 2004 response are reported as the later attributed positions of the heads of the two churches, not as the entry's judgment on the event. The sack's place in the history of the schism is attributed to named holders (Runciman; Bartholomew's reference to 'some historians') and set against the qualifying view that the estrangement was already advanced and was fixed over a longer span (Chadwick), without adjudication. Choniates' account of violence against the city's people is quoted as his eyewitness testimony. SOURCING: the Latin primary lens (Villehardouin, Robert of Clari, Gunther of Pairis) and the Greek primary lens (Choniates) are taken from Dana C. Munro's public-domain translations (Translations and Reprints, vol. 3, no. 1, 1896; rev. ed. 1912) as presented on the Fordham Internet Medieval Sourcebook, read directly and rated high for the quoted passages. Choniates' comparison with the Muslim conquest of Jerusalem in 1187 rests on Magoulias's complete translation, not read line-by-line, and is rated medium. The modern Catholic statement was read directly on the Vatican website, and the Orthodox response (Bartholomew's greeting of 12 May 2004) was read directly in the text published on the joint Catholic-Orthodox Apostolic Pilgrimage website; both are rated high for the quoted passages. Runciman and Chadwick are rated medium, matching their rating elsewhere in the dataset. The academic lens is Queller and Madden, Angold, and Harris, verified to exist and be on-topic through publisher and library records but not read line-by-line, so rated medium; claims resting only on them (the excommunication after Zara, the dates of the coronation, the Latin patriarchate, Innocent III's later reproach and his absolution of the crusaders but not the Venetians, and the historiographical positions summarized) are medium-confidence. No encyclopedias or tertiary sources are cited.

relations.note: Historians such as Steven Runciman, and Ecumenical Patriarch Bartholomew in 2004, describe the sack of 1204 and the installation of a Latin patriarch in Constantinople as deepening the division between the Latin and Greek churches into popular enmity, while others, such as Henry Chadwick, treat it as one stage in an estrangement already advanced and fixed over a longer span.
The Greek Orthodox Church of Constantinople was displaced by a Latin hierarchy from 1204 to 1261, and the sack remains a central memory in Orthodox accounts of relations with the Latin church.

The expedition was proclaimed by Innocent III and its clergy preached the final assault in the pope's name, while the pope himself condemned the attacks on Christians; in 2001 John Paul II expressed the regret of Catholics for the sack.

Alexios Angelos promised to place the Byzantine church under the obedience of Rome, and after the conquest a Latin patriarch subject to the pope was installed in Constantinople; the episode is part of the history of the contested claim to papal primacy in the East.
The Fourth Crusade was a later expedition in the crusading movement begun in 1095; the earlier crusades' passage through Byzantine territory had already strained Latin-Byzantine relations.

The Council of Ferrara-Florence (1438-1445), the late-medieval attempt at reunion of the Latin and Greek churches, met with resistance in the East in which the memory of the Latin conquest of 1204 played a part.

The Byzantine empire restored in 1261 never regained its former extent, and its capital fell to the Ottomans in 1453; Halil Inalcik, following A. M. Schneider, dates the decline of the city from the conquest of 1204.

sources.citation: Choniates, Niketas. O City of Byzantium: Annals of Niketas Choniates, trans. Harry J. Magoulias. Byzantine Texts in Translation. Detroit: Wayne State University Press, 1984. The complete English translation of Choniates' History (1118-1207), including his eyewitness account of the events of 1203-1204 and his contrast between the conduct of the crusaders and that of the Muslim conquerors of Jerusalem in 1187; the Greek primary lens in full. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary translation; underlying Greek text public domain. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Queller, Donald E., and Thomas F. Madden. The Fourth Crusade: The Conquest of Constantinople. 2nd ed. With an essay on primary sources by Alfred J. Andrea. Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1997. Academic monograph reconstructing the diversion as the outcome of a series of contingent decisions rather than a premeditated plan, with a chapter on the sack and the election of the Latin emperor; the academic-history lens on the accident-versus-design debate. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary; cited for reference (author's page for the book), relevant passages not read line-by-line.

Academic study by a Byzantinist setting the Fourth Crusade within the encounter of Byzantium and the West and examining its consequences, including for relations between the churches; the academic-history lens from Byzantine studies. sources.citation: Runciman, Steven. The Eastern Schism: A Study of the Papacy and the Eastern Churches during the XIth and XIIth Centuries. Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1955. The classic scholarly study of the estrangement of Rome and the Eastern churches, arguing that the final breach grew from long divergences of tradition and ideology and was brought to a head by the Norman invasions of Byzantine Italy, the eleventh-century reform of the papacy, and the Crusades; the academic-history lens on the place of the crusades in the schism. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Proprietary (Clarendon Press, 1955); openly borrowable at the Internet Archive. Cited for reference, relevant passages not read line-by-line.

Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2003. Account of the emergence of the division between Rome and Constantinople from apostolic times to the Council of Florence, treating it as a long estrangement rather than the work of a single event; the academic-history lens on the longer span of the schism. Relevant passages not read line-by-line.

sources.citation: Inalcik, Halil. 'The Policy of Mehmed II toward the Greek Population of Istanbul and the Byzantine Buildings of the City.' Trans. from the Turkish by V. L. Ménage. Dumbarton Oaks Papers 23/24 (1969-1970): 229-249. doi:10.2307/1291293. Study by a Turkish historian of the Ottoman Empire of Mehmed II's conduct of the assault and sack under Islamic law, his claim to the Roman imperial throne, the repopulation of Istanbul, and the appointment of Gennadios Scholarios as patriarch; draws on Tursun Beg, Kritovoulos, Doukas, Sphrantzes, and Ottoman archival registers. The modern Muslim scholarly lens. Read directly: the legal rule for a city taken by force and the enslavement of its people (p. 232), the sack, its ending on the first evening (citing Runciman), the 'looted and enslaved city', Tursun Beg's 'my throne is Istanbul', and the Roman imperial claim (p. 233), Kritovoulos on the settlement of the enslaved Greeks (p. 235), and the patriarch's appointment (pp. 236-237).
sources.license: Made freely available by Dumbarton Oaks through the Internet Archive; cited for reference. Relevant passages read directly.
